name: Design an SMS and One-Time-Password Delivery Service
intent: Get a six-digit code onto a user's phone within seconds across unreliable carriers, without sending it twice, without letting it be guessed, and without paying for messages that fraudsters triggered.
codeTitle: routing with failover, a pumping guard and OTP checks
finalIntro: One sign-in code, from the tap on 'send code' to the moment it is entered.
prompt: Design a service that other teams in a company call to send SMS messages, mostly one-time passwords for sign-in and payments. It must pick between several SMS providers, survive a provider outage, report whether each message was delivered, generate and check the codes safely, and not be drained by fraudsters who trigger messages to premium-rate numbers.
functional: Send an SMS to a phone number, and return a message id straight away
Generate a one-time code, send it, and later check the code the user types
Route each message across several providers and fail over when one is unhealthy
Record delivery receipts and let callers read or subscribe to the status of a message
Limit how often codes can be requested, per number and per caller
Report cost per provider and per country
nonFunctional: A code reaches the phone within about 10 seconds for 99% of sends
A client retry or a restart never sends the same message twice
A code is valid for 5 minutes, usable once, and locked after 5 wrong guesses
Survive a full outage of any one provider with no change for callers
Handle hundreds of messages per second at the peak, and absorb bursts
Keep fraud spend small, and never log or store a code in plain text

firstAttempt.text: The login service calls one SMS provider's HTTP API directly. It generates a random code, saves it in the user's row, sends the message, and returns. If the provider call fails, the request fails. The user can ask for a new code as often as they like.
limits: One provider outage means nobody can sign in, and there is no second route
If the call times out, nobody knows whether the SMS was sent, and a retry may send a second one
There is no way to know whether the message arrived, so support can only guess
Anyone can trigger unlimited messages, including to expensive numbers, and the company pays for each
Codes saved as plain text, with no limit on guesses, can be read or brute forced

steps.title: Accept the request, store it, and send from a queue
steps.problem: Calling a provider inside the caller's request ties the user's sign-in to a slow third party, and a timeout leaves it unknown whether the message was sent.
steps.fix: The send API validates the request, writes a message record with a state of 'queued' and a message id, puts the id on a queue in the same step, and returns the id at once. Callers send an idempotency key with each request, and the API stores it with a unique constraint, so a retried request returns the original message id instead of creating a second one. Workers read the queue, and each message is submitted to a provider once per attempt.
steps.tradeoff: Callers never wait for a carrier, bursts are absorbed by the queue, and a retry is safe. The message now has a lifecycle to track, and a code sent a few seconds late may arrive after the user gave up, so urgent messages need their own high-priority queue and a short time to live.

steps.title: Generate, store and check the codes safely
steps.problem: A six-digit code has only a million values, so it is weak by itself, and a stored plain-text code can be read from a database or a log.
steps.fix: The OTP service draws the code from a cryptographic random generator and stores only a salted keyed hash of it, together with an expiry of 5 minutes, a counter of attempts and a used flag. Checking a code compares hashes in constant time, adds one to the counter, allows 5 wrong guesses and then locks the code, and marks it used on success so it works once. Asking for a new code replaces the old one. Requests for codes are limited per number, for example one every 30 seconds and 3 per hour. The code itself is never logged.
steps.tradeoff: A leaked database does not reveal live codes, and guessing is limited to 5 in a million, about 0.0005%, per code. A user who mistypes five times must request a new code, and the limits cost some legitimate users a little patience.

steps.title: Route across providers and fail over
steps.problem: Any one provider has outages, slow routes to some countries and a quality that changes during the day.
steps.fix: A router sits between the queue and the providers. For each message it ranks the providers that serve the destination, and tries the best one. If the provider rejects the message, times out or has an open circuit breaker, it moves to the next. Each provider has a breaker that opens after a few failures in a row, stays open for a cool-down and then lets a single trial message through. Because the message record has one id, a failover attempt is a new attempt for the same message and not a new message.
steps.tradeoff: An outage of one provider turns into a slightly higher price and a few seconds of delay, instead of failed sign-ins. There are now several provider contracts, sender ids and formats to maintain, and failover after a timeout can occasionally produce two messages, because the first may still be delivered.

steps.title: Track delivery receipts
steps.problem: A provider accepting a message says nothing about whether the phone received it, and many sign-in failures are really failures to deliver.
steps.fix: Providers call a receipt webhook with delivery reports, usually accepted, sent, delivered or failed with a reason. The endpoint verifies the signature, looks up the message by the provider's id, and moves the record forward through its states, ignoring a report that would move it backward and any repeat. A message with no final report after a deadline is marked unknown. Callers read the status, or get a webhook of their own. A message that failed for a reason that suggests retrying on another route goes back to the router.
steps.tradeoff: Delivery rates become measurable by provider, country and hour, which drives routing and support. Receipts arrive late, out of order, duplicated or never, and some carriers never send them, so 'delivered' is evidence and not a promise.

steps.title: Choose providers by cost and quality
steps.problem: Prices differ several times over between providers and countries, but the cheapest route is sometimes the one that delivers least.
steps.fix: A table of price and measured quality per provider and per destination country feeds the router. Quality comes from the receipts, such as the share delivered within 10 seconds over the last 15 minutes, and is smoothed so one bad minute does not flip routes. The router picks the lowest cost among the providers above a quality threshold, and sends a small share of traffic to the others so their numbers stay fresh. Sign-in codes weigh speed heavily, and marketing messages weigh price.
steps.tradeoff: The bill falls without making sign-in worse, and a degrading provider loses traffic automatically. The routing rules need review, a small sample of traffic is deliberately sent on the less preferred routes, and the quality figures are only as good as the receipts.

steps.title: Stop SMS pumping with limits and a conversion guard
steps.problem: Attackers trigger codes to numbers they control in premium ranges and share the revenue with a carrier, and per-number limits do not stop them because every request uses a new number.
steps.fix: The fraud guard sits in front of the API. It limits requests per caller, per IP address and per destination number, and checks the app's own token before anything is sent. The strongest signal is conversion: for each destination country and number range, it tracks what share of codes sent are later entered correctly. If sends to a range are climbing and the verification rate is far below normal, say under 10%, the range is blocked or put behind extra proof such as a challenge, and an alert is raised. Ranges with a high cost and little real traffic can be turned off by default.
steps.tradeoff: The company stops paying for messages that nobody reads, within the first few dozen sends of an attack. Blocking a range can also block real users there, so the rules need a quick override, and attackers adapt by mixing in real-looking traffic.

failures.scenario: A provider goes down in the middle of the evening peak
failures.impact: Messages routed to it time out, sign-ins fail, and workers waste time waiting.
failures.answer: Failures open that provider's circuit breaker after a few attempts, so later messages skip it and go straight to the next provider. A single trial message checks it again after the cool-down. The queue holds the burst while capacity shifts, and an alert tells the on-call engineer.

failures.scenario: A client times out and retries the send request
failures.impact: Without protection the user gets two different codes, and the earlier one stops working.
failures.answer: The retry carries the same idempotency key, so the API returns the original message id and no second message is queued. Inside the pipeline a worker that crashes after submitting a message uses the message id as the provider's reference where supported, so a redelivered queue item is recognised.

failures.scenario: A bot sends thousands of codes to numbers in one premium range
failures.impact: The bill grows by thousands of dollars an hour, and the codes are never entered.
failures.answer: The verification rate for that range drops far below normal while sends rise, so the conversion guard blocks the range, usually after a few dozen messages. Spend alerts by country back this up. Afterwards the range stays blocked until a person reviews it.

failures.scenario: Receipts stop arriving from one provider
failures.impact: Every message looks undelivered, so quality figures collapse and the router moves traffic away from a healthy provider.
failures.answer: A drop in receipts without a drop in submit errors is treated as a monitoring gap and not as bad delivery: the router holds its previous quality figures for that provider and raises an alert. Messages with no final report are marked unknown rather than failed.

failures.scenario: An attacker tries all million codes for one number
failures.impact: With unlimited guesses a six-digit code would be found quickly.
failures.answer: Each code allows 5 wrong guesses and then locks, requesting a new code is itself rate limited, and every failed check is counted per account and per IP address. Together this keeps the chance of success tiny and sets off an alert.

alternatives.title: How to reach providers

options.name: A single provider
options.pro: Simplest to run, with one contract and one format
options.con: An outage or a bad route to one country takes sign-in down

options.name: Several providers with failover
options.pro: Survives outages and lets you buy each route at its best price
options.con: More contracts, more formats and a router to operate

options.name: An aggregator that routes for you
options.pro: Fast to start, with someone else managing carriers
options.con: A hidden margin, and less control and visibility

alternatives.pick: Two or three direct providers behind our own router, and an aggregator as one of them if needed.

alternatives.title: How to check a code

options.name: Store a hash of the code and compare
options.pro: Simple, and works with any delivery channel
options.con: The service holds state for every code

options.name: Time-based codes from an authenticator app (TOTP)
options.pro: No SMS cost and no SIM-swap exposure
options.con: Users must set up an app, and recovery is harder

options.name: Passkeys instead of codes
options.pro: Resistant to phishing and no per-message cost
options.con: Needs device support and a fallback path

alternatives.pick: Hashed codes over SMS for reach, with passkeys or TOTP offered as the safer choice.

alternatives.title: How to stop pumping

options.name: Per-number and per-IP limits only
options.con: Bots rotate numbers and addresses, so it only slows them

options.name: A conversion-rate guard per range
options.pro: Catches an attack by its effect on the bill, whatever the technique
options.con: Needs a warm-up and can block a real surge

options.name: Block risky countries
options.pro: Immediate and complete for those countries

alternatives.pick: Limits for the basics, a conversion guard as the main defence, and country blocks as a blunt last resort.

alternatives.title: How to pick the route

options.name: Always the cheapest
options.con: Slow or failed delivery costs more in lost sign-ins

options.name: Cheapest above a quality threshold
options.con: Needs measured quality and a sample of traffic on other routes

options.name: Always the fastest
options.con: Pays a premium for messages that do not need it

alternatives.pick: Cheapest above a quality bar for sign-in codes, and cheapest overall for low-priority messages.
